steps: Non-competitive inhibitors inhibit enzymes without attaching to the active site.
They bind to another part of the enzyme and change the shape of its active site, so the substrate cannot bind properly.
items.finalAnswer: Non-competitive inhibitors bind away from the active site and alter its shape.

steps: Competitive inhibitors have a shape similar to the substrate and compete with it for the enzyme’s active site.
Their binding prevents the substrate from binding; increasing the substrate concentration can reduce their effect.
Non-competitive inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site.
This changes the shape of the active site and reduces enzyme activity; increasing the substrate concentration does not overcome their effect.
items.finalAnswer: Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site, whereas non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the active site’s shape.

steps: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
Most enzymes are proteins.
Enzymes are specific: each enzyme acts on a particular substrate or catalyses a particular reaction.
They are not used up during reactions and can be used again.
Enzymes work effectively in small amounts.
Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and an optimum pH at which it works fastest.
items.finalAnswer: Enzymes are specific protein biological catalysts that can be reused and work best at an optimum temperature and pH.

steps: At low temperatures, enzyme and substrate molecules move slowly, so fewer successful collisions occur and the reaction rate decreases.
As temperature rises, molecules move faster and the reaction rate increases up to the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
Above the optimum temperature, heat disrupts the bonds that maintain the enzyme’s shape.
The active site changes shape, so the substrate no longer fits; the enzyme is denatured and its activity decreases or stops.
Very low temperatures usually slow enzyme activity but do not denature the enzyme.
items.finalAnswer: Low temperatures slow enzyme activity, while high temperatures can denature the enzyme by changing the shape of its active site.

steps: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest.
A change in pH from the optimum reduces the enzyme’s activity.
Very high or very low pH can alter the enzyme’s shape, including the active site, so the substrate cannot bind properly.
At extreme pH, the enzyme may be denatured and stop working.
items.finalAnswer: Enzymes work best at their optimum pH; extreme pH can change the active site and denature the enzyme.

steps: Temperature affects the rate of enzyme activity: activity increases up to the optimum temperature, but high temperatures can denature the enzyme.
pH affects enzyme activity; each enzyme has an optimum pH, and extreme pH can alter its shape.
Increasing substrate concentration increases the reaction rate while enzyme active sites are available; the rate eventually levels off when all active sites are occupied.
Increasing enzyme concentration increases the reaction rate when enough substrate is available.
Inhibitors decrease enzyme activity: competitive inhibitors block the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change its shape.
items.finalAnswer: Enzyme activity is affected by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration and inhibitors.

steps: In the Lock-and-Key model, the active site has a fixed shape that exactly fits a particular substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; the reaction occurs and the products are released.
In the Induced Fit model, the active site is not an exact rigid fit before binding.
When the substrate binds, the enzyme changes shape slightly so that the active site fits the substrate more closely.
Both models explain enzyme specificity and the formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.
items.finalAnswer: The Lock-and-Key model has a fixed active site that fits the substrate, while the Induced Fit model has an active site that changes shape to fit it.
